audit.recode_to: Keep lexical for now. After reading Hess 1977 and Snyder 1968 sec. 1.2 in full, reconsider a root-initial (first-syllable) default with lexically/morphologically contrastive root-vs-suffix placement, if Hess states a Southern rule mirroring the Northern 'first full vowel, else first schwa' generalization (Zahir 2018:27 'Southern Lushootseed tends to stress the first syllable of a word' points the same way).
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: the record's p. 6 quotation is StressTyp2's wording, not Snyder's. IA full-text highlights of the scanned volume confirm sentence 1 verbatim at sec. 1.2 (p. 6 per TOC) and show sentence 2 actually reads 'the meaning of a word may be altered if stress is transferred from the root to a following suffix' — same substance, different words; the pp. 8/19/61 snippets are verbatim in the held Google JSON. sources.quote: 'Stress placement differs between the two dialects as well, in that Northern Lushootseed tends to stress the second syllable of word and Southern Lushootseed tends to stress the first syllable of a word (3). Note that unstressed vowels sometimes reduce to /ə/' with pairs N bədáʔ : S bə́dəʔ 'one's own child', N sqʷəbáyʔ : S sqʷábayʔ 'dog', N dəgʷí : S də́gʷi 'you'. No further stress analysis in the phonology overview.

sources.note: Per Bianco 1995 (held, lush1252) Hess states that stress placement is the primary N/S dialect difference and that the two stress patterns 'are often mirror images' (N = first full vowel of stem, else first schwa); this is the only comparative statement of a Southern stress RULE and could move our lexical coding toward a root-initial default with lexical/morphological exceptions.
